segments.title: Relearning UAD after a major systems update
segments.body: The stream resumes a British campaign begun specifically to explore a heavily changed version of the game. Strategic and tactical play are combined, with new ship designs tested while a worldwide fleet is directed. The opening constraint is domestic unrest rather than a lack of naval strength. Expansion, research, and fleet movements therefore have to support political stability as well as battlefield success.

evidence.note: He explains why the campaign was started and identifies unrest as the immediate strategic constraint.

segments.summary: The campaign tests how ship design and strategy must adapt to Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts' revised systems.

segments.title: Research priorities for a battleship-led campaign
segments.body: Internal protection, boilers, machinery, and hull strengthening take priority for a battleship-centered fleet. Cruiser research is set aside because this campaign is intended to test battleships rather than repeat the earlier battlecruiser approach. Protection and propulsion are treated as enabling technologies rather than isolated upgrades. The research plan follows the kind of fleet the campaign is meant to build and sustain.

evidence.note: He moves research from cruiser design to internal protection and boilers.
He reviews machinery and hull strengthening, then restates that this is the battleship run.

segments.summary: The campaign's research plan shifts toward protection, machinery, and battleship development while older forces cover a worldwide war.

segments.title: Could viewers compete for warship design contracts?
segments.body: Viewers could compete for destroyer or capital-ship contracts, with the preferred design entering the campaign. Rival audience shipyards would answer a stated requirement and have their proposals judged as a procurement competition. Practical rules would be needed so novelty designs do not overwhelm the exercise. The format remains a future project until both the submission rules and the practical circumstances are settled.

evidence.note: He considers the viewer-design proposal and explains why it needs rules.
He responds positively to the competing-shipyards variation.

segments.summary: A viewer proposes a campaign in which rival audience shipyards submit designs, prompting a discussion of rules and procurement-style competition.
segments.question: Could viewers design ships and compete for construction contracts in a future campaign?
segments.answerShort: Possibly: he likes competitive viewer shipyards, but would first define rules that keep submitted designs usable rather than purely comic.

segments.title: How government exploration lowers risk for private spaceflight
segments.body: Private firms rarely lead pure exploration because the distant payoff cannot normally support the initial risk. Governments instead fund the technological frontier and absorb costs whose benefits may appear only over the long term. Small companies then enter when new capabilities create the possibility of large returns, with bigger firms following or acquiring them as uncertainty falls. SpaceX and Starship belong to that transition from exceptionally costly experimentation toward merely expensive, more usable access to space. The answer concerns public investment, technical maturation, and commercial scaling rather than the result of one launch.

evidence.note: He answers the Starship question by explaining why governments fund exploration before private firms follow.
He places SpaceX on a risk ladder and describes spaceflight costs moving from exceptional toward more usable levels.

segments.summary: A Starship question leads to an institutional explanation of why governments fund frontier exploration before small and then large companies follow.
segments.question: What does the Starship and Super Heavy test suggest about the role of private companies in space exploration?
segments.answerShort: Governments usually finance the high-risk frontier; smaller private firms follow as technology opens commercial opportunities, and larger firms enter once the risk and cost fall.

segments.title: Concentrating submarines and battle fleets across a global empire
segments.body: The campaign map becomes a logistics exercise as submarines are drawn from every base that can spare a few boats. Their operational radii rule out a route that would send a force around South America, demonstrating how geography limits nominally global power. Surface ships are then concentrated into a major formation without stripping every other theater. That concentration is intended to damage Spain's economy and support an invasion of northern Spain.

evidence.note: He draws submarines from bases that can spare them and checks their operating radius.
He forms a major fleet, rejects an impractical route around South America, and states the plan to break Spain's economy.
He selects northern Spain as the invasion target.

segments.summary: Submarines are redistributed from bases that can spare them while heavier forces assemble for invasions against Spain.

segments.title: Why Royal Navy submarines carried E and N designations
segments.body: The designation continues traditional Royal Navy submarine numbering whose origins are placed in the First World War era. Letters and numbers identify boats within a historical class sequence. E2 and N therefore belong to the service's established naming system for early submarines.

evidence.note: He directly answers the question about E and N submarine designations.

segments.summary: A brief answer links letter-and-number submarine names to Royal Navy naming practices established around the First World War.
segments.question: Why do British submarines have designations such as E2 and N?
segments.answerShort: They reflect traditional Royal Navy letter-and-number naming systems that began around the First World War era.

segments.title: Why mixed AI gun batteries weaken fire control
segments.body: The game's AI tends to add a wide variety of calibers instead of selecting a coherent main and secondary battery. A better design chooses the best available guns around a consistent fire-control solution. A focused battery can exploit range and accuracy, while the AI's mixed armament leaves its ships easier to outrange and outshoot. The automated designs have nevertheless improved substantially from earlier versions.

evidence.note: He contrasts AI mixed-caliber designs with focused batteries and fire-control needs.

segments.summary: The game's AI favors many gun types instead of coherent batteries optimized for fire control.

segments.title: Using fleet tonnage to dominate Caribbean invasions
segments.body: Battleships, destroyers, cruisers, and submarines are committed to turn a Cuban invasion into an overwhelming operation. The required tonnage is compared with the force already present, and more ships are added until the success probability reaches the desired level. Dispersed naval power has to be concentrated locally before it can support an amphibious campaign. Cuba is also part of a wider plan to remove Spain from the Caribbean and gain the strategic benefits of regional control.

evidence.note: He launches the Cuban invasion and compares required with committed tonnage.
He shifts additional light forces and submarines to support the campaign.

segments.summary: The British fleet masses far more tonnage than required to seize Cuba and prepare further operations against Spanish possessions.

segments.title: Why wars cluster around canals, ports, and maritime communications
segments.body: Communications are the first part of the answer: canals and ports organize the routes on which military and economic movement depends. Water also provides a naturally low-friction surface for carrying heavy and bulky cargo. Equivalent overland movement demands durable roads, bridges, and much more built infrastructure. Conflicts therefore cluster around maritime chokepoints because control of them shapes military mobility and the economic flows that sustain war.

evidence.note: He answers that communications are the central reason.
He explains the transport advantages of water for heavy and bulky loads.

segments.summary: A viewer's question about conflict around canals and ports leads to a compact explanation of communications and low-friction bulk transport by water.
segments.question: Why do so many conflicts center on canals, ships, and ports?
segments.answerShort: Because they control communications and enable heavy or bulky cargo to move with much less friction and infrastructure than overland transport.

segments.title: Sherbrooke as a model for aggressive destroyer raiding
segments.body: Robert Sherbrooke is a stronger fit than Philip Vian for the imagined raiding role. The joking description of Sherbrooke as the more piratical figure matches the premise of attacking Spanish treasure traffic. Senior officers associated with the Tribal-class destroyer force also had the experience and temperament for such a mission. The playful scenario points toward Royal Navy destroyer leadership in the late 1930s.

evidence.note: He names Sherbrooke and comments on the Tribal force's officers.

segments.summary: Robert Sherbrooke and the aggressive culture of Tribal-class officers suit an imagined late-1930s raiding mission.
segments.question: Which late-1930s Royal Navy captain would suit a raiding role against Spanish treasure traffic?
segments.answerShort: Robert Sherbrooke is his preferred example, with Tribal-class senior officers generally well suited to the aggressive role.

segments.title: Ridicule as psychological warfare against Russian prestige
segments.body: An in-game reference to special military operations opens a discussion of ridicule as psychological warfare. Russia's national self-image makes being publicly laughed at especially damaging to political prestige in this interpretation. Ukrainian humor can therefore weaken the intended authority of official language by recasting the invasion as incompetence or farce. Games and popular culture may reinforce that effect even when they are not consciously designed as part of an information campaign.

evidence.note: He connects Ukrainian humor, Russian national image, and ridicule as psychological warfare.

segments.summary: An in-game phrase prompts an explanation of how Ukrainian humor can attack Russia's political image by making official claims look absurd.

segments.title: Building a submarine cordon around Russian routes
segments.body: Submarines and surface ships move toward chokepoints from Singapore to the Kiel Canal and Baltic approaches. Dispersed overseas bases create a cordon rather than support one immediate fleet battle. The stated route to victory is to damage the Russian economy and keep its warships inside their ports. Newly conquered territory, including control of the Kiel Canal approaches and the Russian Far East, changes which bases and routes can support that containment strategy.

evidence.note: War begins and he describes wrecking the Russian economy by blocking ports.
He positions submarines around the Kiel Canal and Baltic routes and plans a Russian invasion.

segments.summary: War with Russia prompts a global redeployment designed to block key ports, contain the Baltic Fleet, and attack economic capacity.

segments.title: Why destroyers and light cruisers converge over time
segments.body: Later destroyers become much faster and more capable. Improvements in machinery, hulls, and armament let them assume missions once reserved for larger scouts and light cruisers. The boundary between the two types consequently becomes less distinct as the campaign advances. Warship classifications describe changing bundles of capability rather than permanent technical categories.

evidence.note: He answers that later destroyers and light cruisers increasingly merge.

segments.summary: A brief design observation explains how increasing destroyer speed and capability narrow the distinction from light cruisers.
segments.question: Do destroyers become more useful and much faster as the campaign advances?
segments.answerShort: Yes; later destroyers improve substantially, and their capabilities increasingly converge with those of light cruisers.

segments.title: University teaching should build independent judgment
segments.body: University education should not lead students toward a prescribed right way of thinking. Teachers provide concepts, evidence, and critical skills that students can use to educate themselves. That purpose differs from rote delivery followed by regurgitation in an examination. A lecture is a one-sided discussion and a seminar a two-way discussion, so both should cultivate judgment rather than obedience.

evidence.note: He contrasts prescribed answers and rote learning with critical thinking, lectures, and seminars.

segments.summary: University teaching should develop independent critical thought instead of leading students toward a prescribed answer.

segments.title: A modernized battle line overwhelms Russian pre-dreadnoughts
segments.body: Battleships form a battle line, cruisers screen them, and destroyers scout ahead. The opposing Russian force can make only 18 knots, which is merely the British line's cruising speed. That mobility advantage allows the faster ships to control the range before bringing heavy guns and dense secondary batteries into action. Repeated design and refit choices produce a tactical overmatch, with the enemy force marked for destruction before its largest harbor is blockaded.

evidence.note: He orders the battle line and screens, demonstrates the volume of fire, credits repeated upgrades, and states his blockade plan.
He identifies the Russian ships as pre-dreadnought equivalents and compares their 18-knot top speed with his battle line's cruising speed.

segments.summary: A tactical battle demonstrates the advantage of speed, long-range gunnery, and coordinated screens against slow Russian capital ships.

segments.title: Which Royal Navy names carry first-rate prestige?
segments.body: Names previously borne by first-rate ships are natural candidates for the Royal Navy's most important new vessels. Warspite belongs in that high-prestige group because of the name's long service associations. Dreadnought carries similar weight through repeated use and its connection with transformative capital ships. Queen Elizabeth is another name that returns across generations as the service revives titles associated with national and naval importance.

evidence.note: He lists prestigious, recurring Royal Navy names.

segments.summary: Warspite, Dreadnought, and Queen Elizabeth are recurring high-prestige Royal Navy ship names.
segments.question: Which Royal Navy names have prestige comparable to the United States Navy's original six frigate names?
segments.answerShort: Names associated with first rates rank highly; he specifically includes Warspite, Dreadnought, and the repeatedly revived Queen Elizabeth.

segments.title: A modified Trieste LHD for Royal Navy amphibious aviation
segments.body: The proposal combines aviation and well-dock capacity in three modified Trieste-class landing helicopter docks. A ski jump would let each ship operate a limited fixed-wing group as well as helicopters and landing craft. Paired with new logistic ships, the LHDs could anchor balanced northern and southern littoral groups and support brigade-scale operations. The third group would provide a reduced carrier capability when both Queen Elizabeth-class carriers are unavailable, or add capacity during a larger crisis.

evidence.note: He develops the three-ship modified Trieste force-structure proposal.

segments.summary: Three ski-jump-equipped Trieste derivatives could replace Ocean, Albion, and Bulwark while backing up the carriers.
segments.question: Would a modified Trieste-class LHD be a good replacement for HMS Ocean?
segments.answerShort: Yes; three ski-jump-equipped derivatives could replace Ocean, Albion, and Bulwark while providing amphibious lift and limited carrier backup.

segments.title: Command initiative should prevent fleet collisions
segments.body: Ships blindly colliding during formation maneuvers recall the lesson associated with HMS Victoria's loss. That disaster demonstrated the danger of treating an admiral's maneuvering order as a substitute for judgment. A Royal Navy captain remains responsible for the safe navigation of the ship under command. The order to move from one station to another therefore does not remove the duty to act and prevent a collision.

evidence.note: He contrasts game behavior with historical command responsibility after HMS Victoria.

segments.summary: Game collisions prompt a historical point about captains' duty to use judgment rather than slavishly follow orders into danger.

segments.title: Slava's historical reputation amid a virtual fleet defeat
segments.body: The game's Slava, Poltava, Chesma, and other ships succumb to concentrated British fire. Ammunition loss, fires, and the speed mismatch make the virtual defeat effectively final. The historical Slava had a much better reputation than this outcome suggests and is described here as one of the Russian Navy's more capable fighters. That distinction keeps the game result separate from the record of the real vessel.

evidence.note: He comments on Slava's historical quality while the Russian squadron is sunk.

segments.summary: As the Russian squadron is destroyed, Slava's reputation as a capable and determined fighting ship separates history from the game result.

segments.title: Why capturing an enemy fleet may be a liability
segments.body: The joke is that the real question is whether the Russian fleet is worth stealing. Captured ships would bring their existing design weaknesses into the victor's inventory and would then need refitting or scrapping. Building ships to domestic standards at overseas stations is preferable even when captured vessels can technically be refitted. In campaign terms, cash or territory therefore offers more strategic value than a collection of poorly matched AI-designed prizes.

evidence.note: He answers the Copenhagen question and explains his preference for cash or territory.
He confirms captured ships can be refitted but still prefers building his own ships at overseas stations.

segments.summary: A Copenhagen-style fleet seizure sounds attractive until the victor must maintain or scrap badly designed captured ships.
segments.question: Can the campaign reproduce Copenhagen by seizing the Russian fleet?
segments.answerShort: Perhaps, but money or territory is preferable because captured AI-designed ships are usually poor assets that must be refitted or scrapped.

segments.title: Why new warships may need an immediate refit
segments.body: A ship can already lag current technology by the time a long construction period ends. The new battleships will therefore enter refit as soon as they join the fleet instead of treating completion as the end of development. Real warships likewise pass through trials that expose defects and reveal changes needed for reliable operation. Post-trial work can correct those faults while installing the best equipment available before the ship begins sustained deployments.

evidence.note: He explains why newly completed ships can immediately enter refit after trials.

segments.summary: An immediate in-game refit reflects the real gap between a ship's design date, trials, and entry into operational service.

segments.title: Rebuilding the Renown class for speed, range, and protection
segments.body: The Renown design converts to oil fuel and improved turbines so it can reach 28 knots. Ammunition, anti-flooding protection, steering gear, and armor are upgraded while displacement and weight balance remain under review. Extra secondary guns use the remaining capacity without sacrificing the intended long range. The completed refit treats speed, protection, firepower, endurance, and stability as one naval-architecture problem rather than independent improvements.

evidence.note: He selects machinery, weapons, protection, and armor for the refit.
He balances secondary armament and displacement before saving the design.

segments.summary: A detailed refit trades added displacement for oil firing, 28-knot speed, stronger protection, improved steering, and longer range.

segments.title: Why Russian warship maintenance repeatedly suffers
segments.body: Money, doctrine, corruption, and competition with the army all contribute to poor Russian ship condition. The central explanation is infrastructure spread across fleets in widely separated theaters. Facilities that look adequate on paper may be badly located or fail to place related repair capabilities together. Limited funding then prevents the state from expanding and connecting those facilities, turning geography and institutional weakness into recurring readiness problems.

evidence.note: He answers the maintenance question by emphasizing dispersed and underfunded infrastructure.

segments.summary: Money, doctrine, corruption, and geography all contribute to poor Russian ship condition, with infrastructure at the center of the answer.
segments.question: Why has Russia so often treated or maintained its warships badly?
segments.answerShort: Money, doctrine, corruption, dispersed fleets, and inadequate ports all matter, but the central problem is poorly located infrastructure that Russia often cannot afford to expand.

segments.title: Balancing battleship numbers, cruiser shortages, and yard capacity
segments.body: The fleet has reached 39 battleships but remains short of light cruisers. A temporary monthly deficit is accepted while submarines are built and capital ships move through lengthy refit queues. Shipyard capacity expands at the same time so future construction is not trapped behind the current program. Capital-ship numbers alone do not create a balanced fleet when screens, money, maintenance time, and industrial capacity lag behind.

evidence.note: He reviews the battleship total, cruiser shortage, and negative balance.
He blocks a port and expands shipyard capacity.

segments.summary: With 39 battleships but too few light cruisers, the campaign exposes the tension between fleet balance, refit queues, and construction capacity.

segments.title: Researching an unwanted caliber to unlock better guns
segments.body: Fourteen-inch guns are not the preferred armament for these battleships. Research into the caliber continues because progress in that branch also improves or unlocks other naval guns. The decision separates the value of a research program from the immediate value of the weapon named on the technology tree. Dependencies can force a navy to fund an intermediate step that does not match its preferred armament policy.

evidence.note: He explains that he would skip 14-inch guns except for the benefits their research provides to other gun development.

segments.summary: Fourteen-inch-gun research continues for the advances it unlocks, even though the fleet is meant to standardize on heavier weapons.

segments.title: Standardizing older battleships around 28 knots
segments.body: Older battleships convert to oil fuel and improved turbines so they can reach a common 28-knot standard. The displacement released or added by the refit goes into stronger belt protection, improved guns, and better internal arrangements. A second class receives the same treatment, including an emphasis on improved 12-inch weapons. Standard speed lets these ships operate with the modernized fleet instead of becoming tactically isolated by slower machinery or obsolete batteries.

evidence.note: He upgrades machinery, speed, armor, and guns on the first class.
He repeats the process on another class and emphasizes 12-inch standardization.

segments.summary: Two capital-ship refits seek common speed, protection, and gun standards so older designs can remain useful with the main fleet.

segments.title: Motor torpedo boat crews and improvised firepower
segments.body: Some reports of British coastal-force attacks made observers wonder whether the boats had somehow acquired 8-inch guns. The boats did not literally carry a normal cruiser battery, but crews explored unusual ways to mount and employ powerful weapons. One-shot kills could therefore produce effects that appeared disproportionate to the size of the attacking craft. The anecdote captures the striking firepower and improvisational culture associated with aggressive motor torpedo boat crews.

evidence.note: He discusses reports of motor boats apparently achieving effects associated with much heavier guns.

segments.summary: A joking gun proposal recalls reports that British motor torpedo boats sometimes appeared to hit with weapons far heavier than they carried.

segments.title: Cruiser refits expose speed and armament tradeoffs
segments.body: New machinery immediately pushes the older cruiser designs overweight. Reducing speed frees capacity, but it also means some cruisers can no longer keep pace with the faster capital ships they may need to support. Existing five-inch batteries remain where six-inch replacements will not fit, while weapons and protection are added within the remaining margin. Pitch, roll, fore-and-aft balance, and armor changes explain why a refit can improve readiness without producing an ideal modern ship. The inherited hull forces compromises among speed, firepower, protection, and fleet role.

evidence.note: He reduces cruiser speed to control machinery weight and works through gun, armor, stability, and balance changes.
A second cruiser refit again trades speed, secondary armament, armor, and weight distribution.

segments.summary: Successive cruiser refits trade speed against machinery weight, gun upgrades, armor, and stability when the older hulls cannot accept every desired improvement.

segments.title: A twelve-gun Queen Elizabeth-class counterfactual
segments.body: The playful counterfactual prefers 16.5-inch weapons to the 14-inch caliber under discussion. It redesigns the Queen Elizabeth class with four triple turrets, producing a twelve-gun heavy battery. Such a layout would be a radical departure from the historical class rather than a minor caliber substitution. Changing gun size and turret arrangement on that scale would reshape displacement, balance, protection, and the international response to the ships.

evidence.note: He imagines the Queen Elizabeth class carrying four triple 16.5-inch turrets and jokes about the reaction abroad.

segments.summary: A Queen Elizabeth design rebuilt around four triple 16.5-inch turrets would radically alter the dreadnought competition.

segments.title: Why coastal-force improvisations are hard to document
segments.body: Coastal forces combined Home Guard-style ingenuity with young crews selected for aggression and initiative. Their experiments could include schemes such as stretching a net between boats to catch enemy E-boats. Not every idea reached operational use, but the proposals reveal how small-craft warfare rewarded improvisation. The crews were not known for preserving complete records, leaving many plausible stories impossible to prove conclusively.

evidence.note: He describes net experiments, aggressive crews, and their improvisational culture.
He explains that weak recordkeeping makes many stories difficult to prove.

segments.summary: Motor-boat crews combined Home Guard-style ingenuity with aggressive initiative, but weak records leave many colorful ideas difficult to verify.

segments.title: Canada, wartime conduct, and Geneva folklore
segments.body: The answer first notes that modern war-crime categories were articulated comparatively recently. Canada is then jokingly identified as the Allied country most associated with stories of conduct that later lawyers would have to address, with New Zealand offered as another candidate. The exchange is military folklore and humor rather than a documented ranking of Allied violations. It distinguishes violence in wartime, the legal language available at the time, and retrospective stories about why later rules exist.

evidence.note: The Home Guard question prompts his distinction between wartime acts and comparatively recent formal war-crime categories.
He jokingly identifies Canada, with New Zealand also suggested, and describes lawyers writing later rules around the folklore.

segments.summary: A darkly comic question about Home Guard tactics leads to a caution about the late formalization of war-crime rules and Canada's popular military reputation.
segments.question: Would improvised Home Guard tactics have been treated as Geneva Convention violations, and which Allied force generated the most such folklore?
segments.answerShort: Modern war-crime law was formalized relatively recently, and Canada is jokingly identified as the Allied force most associated with stories of rules being written afterward.

segments.title: Choosing Chinese invasion targets by port and economic value
segments.body: When war begins with China, the opponent's most important economic and port position is identified before ships are moved. Shanghai stands out for its port capacity, making eastern China the intended invasion target. Submarines already spread across the region can pressure maritime movement while a task force supplies the tonnage needed for the operation. Completed battleship refits then promise to turn economic targeting and sea control into direct amphibious support.

evidence.note: He identifies Shanghai and eastern China as economically and logistically valuable targets.
He links the invasion to completed refits, submarines, and a newly assigned task force.

segments.summary: A new war with China sends submarines and task forces toward Shanghai and eastern China, chosen for port capacity and economic value.

segments.title: Different warships reward different command personalities
segments.body: One aggressive coastal-force temperament would not suit every light cruiser and destroyer command. Different ship types and missions reward different combinations of judgment, patience, initiative, and appetite for risk. Naval services benefit when officers naturally gravitate toward platforms that suit their personalities and skills. Forcing every command into the same mold instead creates the organizational equivalent of putting a square peg into a round hole.

evidence.note: He answers the suggestion by explaining the fit between platform, mission, and personality.

segments.summary: A proposal to give every small combatant a motor-boat mentality prompts a warning that ships and missions require different personality types.
segments.question: Should all Allied light-cruiser and destroyer commands adopt the mentality of motor torpedo boat crews?
segments.answerShort: No; different ships attract and require different personalities, and forcing the same aggressive type into every command creates problems.

segments.title: Heavy-bomber efficiency versus battleship firepower
segments.body: Heavy bombers did not always require the newest engines because several proven engines could move a large payload efficiently. The more important improvements were larger bombs and airframes designed to perform at altitudes beyond the most effective reach of defending fighters. The B-29 demonstrates the value of high-altitude performance rather than engine substitution alone. Against a battleship's sustained shell weight, however, even a large bomber delivers a comparatively limited mass of explosives in each sortie.

evidence.note: He answers the Griffon-Lancaster proposal and compares bomber payload with battleship firepower.
He emphasizes bomb development and high-altitude aircraft performance.

segments.summary: A Lancaster design question leads to a comparison between efficient multi-engine bombers, high-altitude performance, and battleship shell delivery.
segments.question: Would a Barnes Wallis-designed Lancaster with Rolls-Royce Griffon engines have been substantially better?
segments.answerShort: Not necessarily: heavy bombers benefited more from efficient multi-engine production, larger bombs, and high-altitude performance than from simply fitting the latest engines.

segments.title: Designing the Bristol light cruiser to fill a fleet gap
segments.body: The Bristol is designed because the campaign's large battle fleet has an acknowledged shortage of light cruisers. The 9,000-ton hull receives six-inch guns, torpedoes, selected machinery, and as much belt and deck protection as it permits. Pitch, roll, fore-and-aft balance, and an armament heavier than strictly necessary remain compromises in the finished design. Roughly 90,000 tons of spare yard capacity allows ten ships to be ordered. The operational fleet gap is addressed through linked naval-architecture and industrial decisions.

evidence.note: He establishes the light-cruiser requirement and selects machinery, weapons, torpedoes, and armor.
He evaluates stability and weight, checks yard capacity, and orders ten Bristols.

segments.summary: The stream closes with a new 9,000-ton light cruiser built around six-inch guns, torpedoes, armor, and the realities of remaining yard capacity.
